plan.chapterName: Anton, Bivens, and Davis. Calculus, 10th Edition, Figure 5.2.9
plan.contextChunk: This figure contains two panels, (a) and (b), illustrating the disk method for computing the volume of a solid of revolution. Panel (a): the 2D xy-plane showing region R bounded above by the curve y = f(x), below by the x-axis, and between x = a and x = b; a rotation arrow at x = b indicates revolution about the x-axis. Panel (b): a 3D perspective of the resulting solid; at a generic position x along the axis, a circular disk cross-section is highlighted in blue with radius f(x) labeled, showing that each cross-section perpendicular to the x-axis is a disk of area pi[f(x)]^2. The figure derives the disk method formula V = integral from a to b of pi[f(x)]^2 dx by identifying the cross-sectional area at each x and integrating along the axis of revolution.

elements: x-axis with directional arrow and tick marks
y-axis with directional arrow
2D region R (light blue filled area under the curve)
Curve y = f(x) (solid blue line)
Vertical bounding lines at x = a and x = b
Rotation arrow around the x-axis at x = b (curved arrow)
3D solid of revolution (translucent surface with black silhouette outlines)
End-cap boundary disks at x = a and x = b (transparent with grey outlines)
Highlighted 3D disk cross-section at current x (solid light blue with dark blue edge)
1D vertical line segment at current x (shown in 2D view)
Center point of the highlighted disk on the x-axis (red dot)
Radius line from the center to the edge of the disk
Annotation bracket and label for f(x)
Labels: x, y, a, b, R, y=f(x)

interactions.teaches: Allows inspecting the circular symmetry of the solid of revolution from different angles

interactions.label: View
interactions.teaches: Revolving the flat 2D region around the x-axis creates a 3D volume, transforming 1D vertical segments into 2D circular disks

interactions.label: Function and Bounds
interactions.teaches: The solid's radial profile is determined entirely by the function f(x), and its length by bounds a and b

interactions.label: Disk position x
interactions.teaches: Sweeping the disk along the axis shows that its radius at any position x is exactly the function value f(x), yielding a cross-sectional area of π[f(x)]²

demo_steps.title: 2D Region
demo_steps.narration: The 2D area R is bounded by y = f(x), the x-axis, and the limits a and b. A vertical slice at position x has height f(x).

demo_steps.title: 3D Solid of Revolution
demo_steps.narration: Revolving the region around the x-axis sweeps out a solid. The vertical slice becomes a circular disk.

demo_steps.title: Sweeping the Disk
demo_steps.narration: Moving the disk through the solid demonstrates that at every point, the radius of the cross-section is exactly the function's height f(x).

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: X-axis spans from -1 to 6. Y-axis spans from -3 to 3. The true position of the slice/disk is computed as x_val = a + xFrac * (b - a). Colors: curve and disk edges in dark blue #1a66cc, region R and disk fill in light blue #b3d9ff (semi-transparent in 3D), center point red #e74c3c. In the 2D view (a), render R as a flat filled shape in the XY plane. In the 3D view (b), hide R and show the 3D solid as a very light, semi-transparent surface with visible contour lines.
interactionPlan.notes: Use THREE.LatheGeometry for the 3D solid, generating the profile from points sampled from f(x) between a and b. Rebuild the geometry reactively when equation_input fields change. The viewToggle should smoothly transition the camera (e.g., snapping to a frontal view azimuth 90, elevation 0 for 2D, and returning to perspective for 3D) while toggling visibility of the 2D plane elements versus the 3D solid.

authoredContext:
Let f be continuous and nonnegative on [a, b], and let R be the region that is bounded above by y = f (x), below by the x-axis, and on the sides by the lines x = a and x = b (Figure 5.2.9a). Find the volume of the solid of revolution that is generated by revolving the region R about the x-axis. We can solve this problem by slicing. For this purpose, observe that the cross section
of the solid taken perpendicular to the x-axis at the point x is a circular disk of radius f (x)
(Figure 5.2.9b). The area of this region is
A(x) = π[f (x)]

discrepancies: The 3D axes are skewed diagonally by the perspective camera, whereas the source figure uses a stylized oblique projection that keeps the x-axis perfectly horizontal and y-axis vertical.
The 3D solid is rendered as a filled transparent blue volume, whereas the source figure illustrates a hollow shell with a stark black outline.
The curly bracket is drawn as a fixed path in the xy-plane, causing it to appear distorted and rotated away from the viewer in the 3D perspective view.
The default function y=sqrt(x) produces a strictly concave-down shape, missing the inflection point seen in the source figure's generic curve.
evaluation.notes: The generated figure translates the concept exceptionally well into an interactive 3D model, but diverges visually from the source by using a standard 3D perspective and shaded volumes instead of the original's stylized oblique line-drawing style.
action_items: Change the 3D solid material to a clear/white color with solid black silhouette outlines to match the source figure's hollow illustration style.
Align the curly bracket to face the camera (billboard) or draw it in 2D HTML/CSS so it does not distort in the 3D view.
Change the default function f(x) to a polynomial with an inflection point (e.g., a cubic function) to better match the shape of the source curve.
Ensure the camera angle for the 2D view looks directly at the XY plane (azimuth 0) rather than edge-on.

feedback.rationale: The conceptual translation and interactivity are excellent (scoring 5s), and the remaining issues are purely cosmetic style choices and minor visual alignments, making the current figure good enough to stop iterating.
